title: Bulk storage in Zone B
before:
1. Operate Zone B strictly as the bulk storage zone with high-bay pallet racking under PR-02 Put-away to storage.
2. Store all reserve and bulk stock inside the high-bay racking, which provides 2,400 pallet positions.
3. Place only one pallet identifier per rack position and confirm the booking with the WMS scanner before leaving the bay.
4. Respect the structural limit of each rack bay at all times; each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg.
5. Verify pallet weight before lifting to the beams, because a pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg.
6. Split any consignment that would overload a single bay across two or more bays in the same aisle.
7. Use only the assigned reach trucks for all high-bay movements; the fleet provides 5 reach trucks for the high bays.
8. Observe the rated capacity of the reach trucks at 2.0 t and never attempt to lift heavier unit loads with them.
9. Assign Forklift operators trained on reach trucks to Zone B put-away and retrieval tasks.
10. Keep Stock controllers responsible for monitoring bay utilisation and reporting overloads or damage immediately.
11. Maintain main transport aisles through Zone B at 4.0 m wide and keep them completely clear of staged pallets, wrapping material and handling equipment.
12. Maintain rack storage aisles at 3.0 m wide and prohibit parking or double-staging inside them during put-away.
13. Drive at walking pace when entering a storage aisle and yield to a reach truck already positioned at a bay face.
14. Apply free block stacking only in marked floor areas outside the racking and never inside the storage aisles.
15. Limit any free block stack to 3 pallets high.
16. Limit any free block stack to 3.5 m in height, even where three low pallets would remain below that height.
17. Check stack stability, pallet quality and load overhang before adding the second or third pallet.
18. Report leaning stacks, broken boards or shifted loads to the shift supervisor and do not add further pallets to an unstable stack.
19. Return damaged pallets to the designated area and re-palletise the goods before returning them to Zone B.
20. Complete every put-away under PR-02 Put-away to storage by scanning the final bay location so inventory accuracy remains intact for replenishment and picking.

Zone B feeds the ground-level pick faces in the adjacent zone. Accurate bay discipline here prevents shortages, double handling and unsafe overloads downstream.

Coordinate with maintenance staff when rack impact, bent beams or missing safety pins are found. Isolate the affected bay until it has been inspected and released back to use.

title: Racking care and stock accuracy
before:
1. Keep all bulk pallet stock inside the high-bay racking. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. Place no reserve pallet outside its assigned rack position except under PR-02 Put-away to storage or PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Report any pallet found outside address immediately for rebooking.

The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions. Treat every position as a controlled inventory address. Book each put-away, replenishment removal, and relocation by scanner without delay. Leave no pallet physically moved without a matching system movement.

2. Respect the structural limit of every bay. Each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg. Calculate the bay total from all levels before adding another pallet. Split heavy consignments across adjacent bays rather than concentrating weight in one bay.

Check label weights during PR-02 Put-away to storage and during PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Stop put-away to any bay showing deformation, cracking, or loose fixings. Barricade the affected bay and notify supervision before continuing work in the aisle.

3. Protect uprights, beams, and bracing from impact. Approach bays squarely and lift clear of beams before reversing. Lower pallets centrally onto both support beams. Remove any twisted, broken-board, or overhanging pallet from racking and transfer it for rework.

Never climb racking, store goods directly on bracing, or place loose cartons into a pallet position. Keep rack storage aisles free of empty pallets, stretch film, and debris after each task. Return handling equipment to its parking area when the task ends.

4. Maintain the monthly inspection regime without exception. Racking gets a documented safety inspection every month. Support the inspection by clearing beam levels for visual access and by reporting earlier damage without waiting for the due date.

The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs. Direct all beam damage, missing safety pins, anchor defects, and levelling faults to that route. Prohibit use of any bay marked out of service until the repair log confirms release.

5. Keep rack stock equal to the system at all times. Count from physical stock first under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, then compare with the system figure. Investigate overages as carefully as shortages, including wrong bay, wrong level, and duplicated labels.

Reconfirm any adjusted location by a second physical check before closing the task. Escalate repeated variances at the same address for bay audit, scanner review, and process correction. Release frozen moves only through the authorised procedure.

6. Control housekeeping around the racking footprint. Verify beam signage, bay numbering, and weight notices remain legible. Replace damaged labels through the stock control route rather than handwriting over them. Record every inspection, damage report, repair, and adjustment so the history of each bay remains traceable.

title: Safety inspections and incidents
before:
1. Inspect all pallet racking under a documented safety inspection every month.
Schedule the inspection to cover every aisle in rotation so no bay remains unchecked beyond the monthly interval.
Record beam damage, upright deformation, missing pins, anchor condition and load notices in the inspection log.

2. Verify during each inspection that each rack bay carries at most 2,700 kg.
Compare the displayed bay load against the system weight for the stored pallets.
Mark any overloaded bay out of service immediately until the load is corrected.

3. Assign the physical inspection and follow-up repairs to the maintenance technician.
The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs.
Ensure every defect, adjustment and component replacement appears in the repair log with date and signature.

4. Isolate damaged uprights, bent beams or leaking pallets on discovery.
Unload the affected levels with suitable handling equipment before any repair attempt.
Release the bay back to operation only after the repair log confirms its release.

5. Photograph structural damage before moving stock or starting repairs.
Attach the photographs to the inspection record for traceability.
Retain the records for audit alongside the monthly inspection sheets.

6. Submit an incident report for every near miss, injury, collision, dropped pallet, rack strike or spill.
Complete the report before the end of the shift in which the event occurred.
Include location, equipment involved, persons present and immediate actions taken.

7. Forward every incident report to the on-duty supervisor without delay.
The shift supervisor reviews every incident report.
Do not close the report until the review, root cause and corrective actions are documented.

8. Apply immediate containment after any incident involving racking.
Cordon off the affected bay and adjacent working area with barriers.
Notify downstream operations to reroute put-away, replenishment and picking tasks.

9. Investigate rack impacts jointly with operations and maintenance.
Examine floor markings, handling routes and load condition for contributing factors.
Define retraining, layout changes or additional protection where the findings require it.

10. Track all open inspection findings and incident actions to closure.
Review overdue items at the daily operational meeting until each is signed off.
Escalate any repeat overload, repeat impact or overdue structural repair for management decision.

11. Hand over outstanding defects and open incidents between shifts in writing.
State the bay numbers concerned, the isolation measures in place and the next planned step.
Confirm that the incoming responsible person has understood the restrictions before resuming work nearby.

title: Racking and stacking limits
before:
1. Respect the rated limits of all storage structures in Zone B. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions. Never place more weight or height on racking or floor stacks than this instruction allows, and never climb on racking to reach stock.

2. Limit each rack bay to at most 2,700 kg total load. Calculate the bay total from the gross weight of every pallet level within that bay before putting away the next pallet. Distribute heavy pallets to lower levels where the rack design requires it, and leave any bay showing deflection, cracking or impact damage unloaded until cleared.

3. Keep every pallet within its gross weight allowance. A pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg. Check the system weight or weigh indication before put-away and before replenishment. Reject overweight, unstable or overhanging pallets for rework and do not place them into high-bay positions.

4. Stack free block-stacked pallets only to the permitted height. Free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 3.5 m in height. Free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 3 pallets high. Apply both limits together, so the lower of the two controls the stack. Build stacks square, interlocked and on sound pallets, with heavier units at the base.

5. Maintain clear operating clearances around racking at all times. Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide. Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide. Do not stage pallets, waste, chargers or handling equipment inside these aisles. Keep pallet overhang, stretch film tails and loose strapping outside the aisle profile.

6. Operate handling equipment in racking strictly under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Approach bays squarely, lift and lower smoothly, and confirm adequate headroom before raising a load to height. Stop work immediately if the truck contacts uprights, beams or bracing, barrier off the affected bay, and report the impact without delay.

7. Support the monthly integrity regime for racking. Racking gets a documented safety inspection every month. The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs. Report bent uprights, missing safety pins, damaged beams, loose floor fixings and leaking goods to supervision on the same shift, and do not reload a quarantined bay.

8. Treat any suspect stack as unsafe until examined. Re-stack leaning columns, re-wrap loose loads, and transfer damaged pallets to quarantine under escort. Never pull a pallet from the bottom of a block stack, never stand pallets on edge against racking, and never leave a raised load unattended in the aisle.

title: Forklift Operators
before:
Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks. The role covers pallet movements between receiving, storage, picking, dispatch and value-added areas under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation.

1. Operate only after authorisation. Only the warehouse manager may authorise new forklift operators. No operator starts unsupervised truck work without that authorisation recorded.
2. Complete the documented pre-use check each day. Every forklift gets a documented pre-use check each day, and the daily forklift check happens BEFORE first use each day.
3. Operate the assigned fleet within rated capacity. The fleet has 9 electric counterbalance forklifts rated at 3.0 t, 5 reach trucks for the high bays rated at 2.0 t, 11 electric pallet jacks and 12 hand pallet jacks.
4. Observe site speed limits at all times. Forklifts must not exceed 8 km/h inside the building. Forklifts must not exceed 12 km/h in the outdoor yard.
5. Slow for people and ramps. Forklifts must slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings. Forklifts must not exceed 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches.
6. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Give way on segregated pedestrian walkways which are 1.2 m wide, keep clear of walkway markings, and use the 4.0 m wide main transport aisles for travel and the 3.0 m wide rack storage aisles only at controlled speed.
7. Wear mandatory personal protection on the floor. High-visibility vests are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor. Safety footwear class S3 is mandatory on the warehouse floor. Forklift operators must wear seat belts whenever the truck is moving.
8. Execute put-away and replenishment moves to instruction. Follow PR-02 Put-away to storage for transfers from Zone A to Zone B, and PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces for transfers from bulk storage to Zone C.
9. Serve all operating zones as tasked. Zone A is the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks. Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Zone F holds the value-added services area.
10. Respect storage limits in Zone B. The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions. Each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg. A pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg. Free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 3.5 m in height and must not exceed 3 pallets high.
11. Handle hazardous loads only under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. The hazmat cage is inside Zone F and covers 60 m2. No more than 3,000 kg of hazmat may be stored in the hazmat cage at one time, which holds at most 3 full-weight pallets. Check hazmat cage stock weight before every put-away and reject any receipt exceeding 3000 kg.
12. Report to shift control. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs. Escalate defects, damage and unsafe conditions immediately and stop the affected truck or operation until cleared.

title: Put-away and Storage Accuracy
before:
1. Harborwick 3PL Ltd. commits to accurate put-away of all booked inventory under PR-02 Put-away to storage.
2. Inbound operators unload, count and inspect inbound goods in Zone A before any storage movement begins.
3. Within receiving, inspection of inbound goods is completed before booking into the system.
4. Following system booking, goods are released for put-away to storage without interim diversion.
5. Through this sequence the client receives full system traceability from dock receipt to final storage location.

6. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking.
7. Across that zone the high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions dedicated to client stock.
8. Against every position Harborwick records pallet identity, SKU, quantity and bay location at the time of put-away.
9. Accordingly the client inventory remains system-directed, with no unbooked pallets held in bulk storage.

10. For weight control a pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 800 kg.
11. Beyond pallet level each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg.
12. Inside bulk storage consignments exceeding bay capacity are split before put-away to protect rack integrity.
13. Consequently storage accuracy includes continuous compliance with both pallet and bay weight limits.

14. Where free block stacking applies, stacked pallets must not exceed 3.5 m in height.
15. Separately free block-stacked pallets must not exceed 3 pallets high.
16. Both height and quantity limits are applied together during put-away planning and floor verification.
17. Toward accuracy assurance, any stack found outside either limit is corrected and rebooked before acceptance as stored.

18. Ultimately Harborwick warrants that booked goods are put away to the assigned Zone B location, within stated rack and stacking limits, with system accuracy maintained from booking through storage.
